title: Karen Horney: Neurotic Needs and Trends
overview: Karen Horney trained as a Freudian but broke away over Freud's view of women and his biological emphasis, arguing that social and cultural forces, especially parent-child relationships, shape personality. A child's safety need is frustrated when parents lack genuine warmth; the repressed hostility becomes basic anxiety, against which children protect themselves by securing affection, submitting, seeking power or withdrawing. These defences can harden into ten neurotic needs, which Horney later grouped into three neurotic trends: compliant (toward people), aggressive (against people) and detached (away from people). Neurotics are ruled by one trend and intense conflict, and build an unrealistic idealized self-image that leads to the tyranny of the shoulds and externalization. Her feminine psychology replaced penis envy with womb envy and desexualised the Oedipus complex. The chapter also covers her optimistic view of human nature, her assessment methods, research on neurotic trends, the shoulds and neurotic competitiveness, and an evaluation of her theory.
objectives: Explain how Horney's childhood and cultural setting shaped her break from Freud and her theory.
Describe the childhood safety need, the parental behaviours that undermine it and the four reasons hostility is repressed.
Define basic anxiety and describe the four self-protective mechanisms against it.
List the ten neurotic needs and link them to the three neurotic trends (compliant, aggressive, detached).
Distinguish normal from neurotic people in terms of trend dominance, conflict and the idealized self-image.
Explain the tyranny of the shoulds and externalization.
Outline Horney's feminine psychology: womb envy, flight from womanhood, the reinterpreted Oedipus complex and cultural influences on women.
Describe Horney's image of human nature, her assessment methods and the research evidence for her theory.
Evaluate the contributions and criticisms of Horney's theory.

sections.heading: Horney's Departure from Freud
sections.detailed:
Karen Danielsen Horney is the third neo-psychoanalytic dissenter in the book after Jung and Adler. Unlike them she was never Freud's colleague, but she was trained in orthodox psychoanalysis. She did not stay a Freudian for long, and her split began over one specific issue: Freud's psychological picture of women.

As an early feminist, Horney complained that psychoanalysis had been built around male development. Against Freud's idea that women are driven by penis envy, she proposed the reverse: men envy women because women can give birth. She claimed she had seen just as many men with womb envy as women with penis envy, a remark that displeased Freud and most male analysts.

Two sets of influences shaped her theory. The first was her own childhood and adolescence. The second was the social and cultural setting she worked in. She developed her theory in the United States, a culture very different from Freud's Vienna, and by the 1930s and 1940s attitudes about sex and gender roles had changed a great deal, more in America than in Europe.

A key observation drove her shift. Her American patients differed so much from her earlier German patients, in their neuroses and in their normal personalities, that she concluded only differences in social forces could explain it. If personality were wholly biological, as Freud held, such large cross-cultural differences should not appear.

Like Adler, she therefore gave social relationships and interactions far more weight than Freud did. She denied that sex is the governing force in personality and questioned the Oedipus complex, the libido and the id-ego-superego structure. For Horney, people are driven not by sexual or aggressive instincts but by the needs for security and love, a view that mirrors her own life.
sections.simple: Horney trained as a Freudian but broke away, first over Freud's views on women; she said men have womb envy just as Freud said women have penis envy. Seeing how different her American and German patients were, she decided culture and social relationships, not biology, shape personality. People are driven by needs for security and love, not sex or aggression.
keyPoints: Trained in Freudian theory but never Freud's colleague; broke away over his view of women.
Countered penis envy with womb envy: men envy women's ability to give birth.
Differences between American and German patients convinced her social forces, not biology, shape personality.
Like Adler, stressed social relationships; questioned Oedipus complex, libido and the three-part structure.
Core motives are the needs for security and love, not sex or aggression.

sections.heading: The Life of Horney (1885-1952)
sections.detailed:
Horney's theory grew directly out of her life, so this section is a common 5-mark question (how did her childhood shape her theory?).

A neglected second-born. Karen Danielsen grew up in a village near Hamburg, Germany. She was the second child and envied her older brother Berndt, the charming, adored first-born, even though she was brighter and livelier. She also envied him simply for being a boy at a time when girls were seen as inferior, and admitted she long wished to be a boy. Her father, a 50-year-old ship's captain of Norwegian background, was religious, domineering, imperious and gloomy. Her mother, 17 years younger, was attractive, spirited and freethinking. The parents quarrelled whenever he was home from sea; the mother openly wished him dead and told Karen she had married only to avoid spinsterhood.

A search for love. For much of her youth Horney doubted her parents wanted her and believed they preferred Berndt. At 16 she wrote that she had every beautiful thing on earth except love. She longed for her father's attention, but he frightened her and belittled her intelligence and looks.

Rebellion and hostility. To keep her mother's affection she played the adoring, obedient daughter, and until about 8 she was clinging and compliant. When this did not bring enough love and security, she switched tactics and became ambitious and rebellious, deciding that if she could not be beautiful she would be smart. As an adult she saw how much hostility she had built up, and her theory describes exactly how lack of love in childhood breeds anxiety and hostility. Her biographer Paris concluded that all her writings were an effort to understand and relieve her own difficulties.

Still searching for love. As a teenager she had crushes on teachers; at 17 she had a first love that lasted two days, and another affair filled 76 diary pages. She decided being in love temporarily removed her anxiety and insecurity. Her career, by contrast, went smoothly: kindness from a physician at 12 made her decide to become a doctor, and despite discrimination against women and her father's opposition she entered the University of Freiburg medical school in 1906.

Marriage and career. She married Oskar Horney, a political-science student who became a businessman, and took her medical degree from the University of Berlin in 1913. The early marriage brought misery: three daughters, crying spells, stomach pains, fatigue, compulsions, frigidity and a wish for sleep or death. The marriage ended after 17 years, and she had many affairs, feeling desperate without a man and hating her dependence when with one.

Horney's psychoanalysis. Her analyst Karl Abraham, a Freudian loyalist, traced her problems to Oedipal longings for her powerful father, even reading meaning into her leaving her handbag in his office. The analysis failed, and she turned to self-analysis for the rest of her life. Adler's ideas on compensation for inferiority, especially from physical unattractiveness, struck her: she concluded she needed to feel superior because of her perceived lack of beauty and inferiority as a woman, which led to masculine protest through excelling in medicine, then a male domain.

Later life. In the United States her most intense affair, with analyst Erich Fromm (15 years younger), lasted 20 years; it broke down partly after Fromm analysed her daughter Marriane, who then confronted her mother. She continued relationships with ever younger men, sometimes with detachment. From 1932 to 1952 she taught at psychoanalytic institutes in Chicago and New York, helped found the Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis and the American Institute for Psychoanalysis, and started the American Journal of Psychoanalysis in 1941.
sections.simple: Horney felt unloved as a child: her brother was the favourite and her stern father belittled her. She first tried being a good, compliant girl, then became ambitious and rebellious. Her lifelong hunt for love and security, a failed Freudian analysis and self-analysis all fed straight into her theory.
keyPoints: Second-born; envied brother Berndt; stern, belittling father and unhappy parental marriage.
Compliant till about 8, then ambitious and rebellious: 'if not beautiful, then smart'.
Theory mirrors her life: lack of childhood love produces anxiety and hostility (Paris).
Medical degree, Berlin 1913; unhappy 17-year marriage to Oskar Horney; many affairs.
Failed analysis with Karl Abraham led to lifelong self-analysis; influenced by Adler's inferiority idea.
Founded the American Institute for Psychoanalysis and the American Journal of Psychoanalysis (1941).

sections.heading: The Childhood Need for Safety and Security
sections.detailed:
Horney agreed with Freud on one big point: the early childhood years shape the adult personality. She disagreed on how. For her, social forces in childhood, not biological ones, drive development. There are no universal stages and no inevitable childhood conflicts; the parent-child relationship is what matters.

The safety need. Childhood, she said, is dominated by the safety need, the need for security and freedom from fear. Whether an infant feels secure and unafraid decides whether its personality develops normally. A child's security depends entirely on how its parents treat it, and the main way parents damage security is by failing to show warmth and affection. Horney's own parents gave little warmth, and she later did the same with her daughters. She argued that children can survive many things usually called traumatic, such as abrupt weaning, occasional beatings or even early sexual experiences, provided they feel wanted and loved.

Ways of undermining a child's security. Parents can weaken security, and so provoke hostility, through obvious favouritism toward a sibling, unfair punishment, erratic behaviour, broken promises, ridicule, humiliation and isolating the child from peers. Children can tell whether parental love is genuine; fake displays of affection do not fool them easily.

Repressing hostility toward parents. The child often has to bury the hostility these behaviours create. Horney gave four reasons:

1. Helplessness. Infants depend totally on their parents. Keeping a child overly dependent increases helplessness, and the more helpless the child, the less it dares rebel. In effect: "I must repress my hostility because I need you."

2. Fear. Punishment, physical abuse or subtler intimidation make the child afraid, and the more afraid, the more it represses: "I must repress my hostility because I am afraid of you."

3. Love. Paradoxically, parents may keep telling the child how much they love it and sacrifice for it while their warmth is not sincere. The child sees through this but it is all the love on offer, so it represses hostility rather than lose even this poor substitute.

4. Guilt. Children are made to feel wicked, unworthy or sinful for resenting their parents. The more guilt, the deeper the repression.

This repressed hostility, arising from many parental behaviours, undermines the safety need and shows itself as basic anxiety.
sections.simple: Every child needs to feel safe and free from fear, and that depends on whether parents show real warmth and love. Favouritism, unfair punishment, broken promises, ridicule and the like make the child hostile. The child buries that hostility because it is helpless, scared, afraid of losing what love there is, or guilty, and the buried hostility turns into basic anxiety.
keyPoints: Agreed with Freud that early childhood matters, but said social not biological forces shape it.
Safety need: need for security and freedom from fear; depends entirely on parental treatment.
Main threat to security is lack of genuine warmth and affection; children can tell fake love.
Undermining behaviours: favouritism, unfair punishment, erratic behaviour, broken promises, ridicule, humiliation, isolation.
Hostility is repressed because of helplessness, fear, (insincere) love and guilt.

sections.heading: Basic Anxiety: The Foundation of Neurosis
sections.detailed:
Horney defined basic anxiety as a gradually growing, all-pervading feeling of being lonely and helpless in a hostile world. It is the foundation on which all later neuroses are built, and it is inseparably linked with hostility, helplessness and fear. However it is expressed, the feeling is much the same for everyone: we feel small, insignificant, deserted and endangered in a world that seems ready to cheat, attack, humiliate and betray us.

In childhood we try to protect ourselves against basic anxiety in four different ways.

1. Securing affection. The message is "If you love me, you will not hurt me." Affection can be sought by doing whatever others want, by bribing them, or even by threatening them into giving it.

2. Being submissive. The person complies with the wishes of one particular person or of everyone around. Submissive people avoid anything that might antagonise others; they will not criticise, will not give offence, repress their own wishes and do not defend themselves against abuse for fear of provoking the abuser. Most believe they are unselfish and self-sacrificing. The message is "If I give in, I will not be hurt." This fits Horney's own behaviour until about 8 or 9.

3. Attaining power. Power over others compensates for helplessness and brings security through success or a feeling of superiority: if I have power, no one can harm me. This fits Horney once she turned to academic success.

4. Withdrawing. The first three ways all cope by dealing with other people. The fourth means pulling away from people, psychologically rather than physically, and becoming independent of others for both internal and external needs. Psychological independence comes from becoming aloof and no longer turning to others for emotional needs; these needs are blunted or minimised, and by renouncing them the person guards against being hurt.

Characteristics of the self-protective mechanisms. All four have one goal: defence against basic anxiety. They push the person to seek security and reassurance, not happiness or pleasure; they are a defence against pain, not a pursuit of well-being. They are powerful and intense, possibly more compelling than sexual or other physiological needs. They may reduce anxiety, but usually at the price of an impoverished personality. Neurotics often use more than one mechanism, and because the mechanisms are incompatible (for example wanting both power and affection, or wanting to submit to others while also dominating them) this lays the ground for further, unresolvable and more severe conflicts.
sections.simple: Basic anxiety is a creeping feeling of being alone and helpless in a hostile world, and it is the root of all neurosis. Children defend against it in four ways: getting affection, giving in, gaining power, or pulling away emotionally. These defences buy safety, not happiness, and mixing them creates even more conflict.
keyPoints: Basic anxiety: insidious, all-pervading feeling of loneliness and helplessness in a hostile world; foundation of neurosis.
Four defences: securing affection, being submissive, attaining power, withdrawing.
First three involve dealing with people; withdrawal means psychological (not physical) distance.
Mechanisms seek security, not happiness; can be stronger than sexual needs; cost an impoverished personality.
Using incompatible mechanisms together (e.g., power and affection) produces further severe conflict.

sections.heading: Neurotic Needs
sections.detailed:
Horney argued that any self-protective mechanism can become such a permanent part of personality that it acts like a drive or need directing behaviour. She listed ten of these and called them neurotic needs because they are irrational solutions to a person's problems.

The ten neurotic needs are:
1. Affection and approval
2. A dominant partner
3. Power
4. Exploitation
5. Prestige
6. Admiration
7. Achievement or ambition
8. Self-sufficiency
9. Perfection
10. Narrow limits to life

Link to the four self-protective mechanisms. The needs map onto the four defences. Securing affection appears as the need for affection and approval. Being submissive includes the need for a dominant partner. Attaining power covers the needs for power, exploitation, prestige, admiration, and achievement or ambition. Withdrawing includes self-sufficiency, perfection and narrow limits to life. (A useful memory tip: 1 + 1 + 5 + 3 = 10.)

When is a need neurotic? Horney stressed that everyone shows these needs to some degree; at times we all want affection or chase achievement. None of them is abnormal in a passing, everyday sense. A need becomes neurotic when the person pursues it intensely and compulsively as the only way to resolve basic anxiety. Then it grows more severe and finally tyrannical, taking over and dominating the personality (Hess & Hess).

Why they fail. Satisfying neurotic needs does not make us feel safe; it only lets us escape the discomfort of anxiety for a while. They treat the symptoms, not the cause, and leave the underlying anxiety untouched. And when a need is pursued only to cope with anxiety, the person tends to fix on that one need and seek it compulsively in every situation.
sections.simple: Any of the four defences can harden into a permanent drive. Horney listed ten such neurotic needs, from affection and a dominant partner to perfection and narrow limits to life. Everyone has these needs a bit; they become neurotic when chased compulsively as the only way to handle anxiety, and even then they only ease symptoms, not the anxiety itself.
keyPoints: Neurotic needs: ten irrational defences against anxiety that become permanent parts of personality.
Affection/approval; dominant partner; power; exploitation; prestige; admiration; achievement; self-sufficiency; perfection; narrow limits to life.
Mapping: affection (1), submission (1), power (5), withdrawal (3).
Neurotic only when pursued intensely, compulsively, as the 'only' answer to basic anxiety.
They relieve symptoms, not the underlying anxiety, and are applied rigidly in all situations.

sections.heading: Neurotic Trends: Compliant, Aggressive and Detached Personalities
sections.detailed:
In her later writings (1945) Horney reformulated the ten needs. Her clinical work suggested they fall into three groups, each expressing the person's attitudes toward self and others. She called these three categories of directional movement the neurotic trends. Because they grow out of the self-protective mechanisms they resemble them. They involve compulsive attitudes and behaviours, and they are shown indiscriminately in every situation.

Table 5.1 groups the needs: affection and approval and a dominant partner make up the compliant personality (movement toward people); power, exploitation, prestige, admiration and achievement make up the aggressive personality (movement against people); self-sufficiency, perfection and narrow limits to life make up the detached personality (movement away from people).

The compliant personality (moving toward people). Such people have an intense, constant need for affection and approval, to be loved, wanted and protected. They show this toward everyone but usually need one dominant person, a friend or spouse, to take charge and protect them. They manipulate others, especially partners, by being endearing: considerate, appreciative, responsive, understanding and sensitive. They try to live up to others' expectations and appear unselfish and generous. They are conciliatory, put their own wishes below others', accept blame, defer, and are never assertive, critical or demanding. Their stance toward themselves is helplessness and weakness, as if saying "I am so weak that you must protect and love me." They see others as superior and themselves as inferior even when competent. Because their security depends on others, they become overly dependent, need constant reassurance, and are terrified by any real or imagined rejection, which drives them to win back affection. Underneath lies repressed hostility: Horney found deep defiance, vindictiveness and a wish to control and exploit others, the opposite of what they show. Because these impulses must be held down, they become subservient and ask nothing for themselves.

The aggressive personality (moving against people). For these people everyone is hostile and only the fittest and most cunning survive; life is a jungle where supremacy, strength and ferocity are the top virtues. Their motive is the same as the compliant type's, relief from basic anxiety, but they never show fear of rejection. They are tough, domineering and disregard others. To get the control and superiority they need, they must keep performing at a high level and enjoy having their superiority recognised. They judge every relationship by what they can gain; instead of appeasing, they argue, criticise and demand. They drive themselves to be the best and may be very successful in their careers, but work gives no intrinsic satisfaction; it is only a means to an end. They may seem confident and uninhibited, yet like compliant types they are driven by insecurity, anxiety and hostility.

The detached personality (moving away from people). These people keep emotional distance; they must not love, hate, cooperate or get involved. To manage this they strive for self-sufficiency and need well-developed resources of their own. They have an almost desperate need for privacy, want to be alone as much as possible, and dislike sharing even an experience like listening to music. Their need for independence makes them sensitive to any attempt to influence, coerce or obligate them, so they avoid constraints such as timetables, schedules, marriages, mortgages and even the pressure of a belt or necktie. They need to feel superior, but unlike aggressive types they cannot compete (that means involvement), so they expect their greatness to be recognised automatically; they feel unique and apart from everyone. They suppress or deny feelings, especially love and hate, because intimacy would bring conflict, and they put heavy stress on reason, logic and intelligence.

Link with Adler. The three types resemble Adler's styles of life: compliant is like the getting type, aggressive like the dominant or ruling type, and detached like the avoiding type, another example of Adler's influence.

Comparing aggressive and detached types (a review question). Both feel superior, but the aggressive type earns superiority through competition and achievement and seeks recognition, while the detached type avoids competition and expects recognition without effort. The aggressive type engages with people (against them); the detached type avoids people. The aggressive type is the one more likely to become highly successful in a career, though without intrinsic satisfaction from the work.
sections.simple: Horney later grouped the ten needs into three trends. Compliant people move toward others: they crave love and approval and act weak and pleasing. Aggressive people move against others: life is a jungle, so they fight to win and dominate. Detached people move away: they guard privacy, avoid commitments and lean on logic instead of feelings.
keyPoints: Neurotic trends (1945): three categories of attitudes and behaviour toward self and others; compulsive and indiscriminate.
Compliant (toward): needs affection, approval, a dominant partner; feels helpless; hides repressed hostility.
Aggressive (against): life is a jungle; seeks control, superiority, recognition; can succeed in career without inner satisfaction.
Detached (away): needs privacy, self-sufficiency, freedom from constraints; feels unique; stresses reason over emotion.
Parallels Adler's getting, ruling/dominant and avoiding types.

sections.heading: Dominance of One Trend, Conflict and the Expression of All Three Trends
sections.detailed:
These three short headings explain how the neurotic trends operate together and how a normal person differs from a neurotic one, a frequent exam comparison.

The dominance of one trend. In the neurotic person one trend dominates while the other two are present to a lesser degree. A mainly aggressive person, for instance, still has some need for compliance and detachment. The dominant trend governs the person's behaviour and attitudes toward others because it is the mode that best controls basic anxiety; any departure from it feels threatening. So the other two trends must be actively repressed, which creates further problems, and any sign that a repressed trend is pushing for expression causes inner conflict.

Conflict. In Horney's system conflict means the basic incompatibility of the three neurotic trends, and this conflict is the core of neurosis. Everyone, normal or neurotic, suffers some conflict among these basically irreconcilable modes. The difference is intensity: in the neurotic the conflict is much stronger. Neurotics must fight to keep the non-dominant trends from being expressed. They are rigid and inflexible, meeting every situation with the behaviour of their dominant trend whether or not it fits.

The expression of all three trends. In the person who is not neurotic, all three trends can be shown as circumstances demand: sometimes aggressive, sometimes compliant, sometimes detached. The trends are not mutually exclusive and can be integrated harmoniously. The normal person is flexible and adapts to changing situations.

Summary of normal versus neurotic. Both have all three trends and some conflict. The neurotic is ruled by one dominant trend, represses the others, experiences intense conflict and behaves rigidly. The normal person integrates the trends, uses whichever suits the situation, experiences milder conflict and is flexible.
sections.simple: In neurotics one trend takes over and the other two are pushed down, which causes inner conflict. Everyone has some clash between the three trends, but neurotics feel it much more and respond to every situation in the same rigid way. Normal people use all three trends flexibly, depending on what the situation needs.
keyPoints: Neurotics: one dominant trend; the other two present but actively repressed.
Conflict = the basic incompatibility of the three trends; the core of neurosis.
Normal and neurotic people both have conflict; it is far more intense in neurotics.
Neurotics are rigid, using the dominant trend in every situation regardless of fit.
Normal people express all three trends as needed; the trends are integrated and flexible.

sections.heading: The Idealized Self-Image
sections.detailed:
Horney held that all of us, normal or neurotic, build a picture of ourselves that may or may not match reality. Her own search for self was long and painful; at 21 she described herself as inner chaos, like a face that only took shape in the expression of the moment.

Normal versus neurotic self-image. In normal people the self-image rests on a realistic appraisal of abilities, potential, weaknesses, goals and relations with others. It gives the personality unity and integration and a framework for dealing with self and others. To reach self-realization, the full development of our potential, the self-image must clearly reflect the true self. Neurotics, torn by incompatible modes of behaviour, have disunited, disharmonious personalities. They build an idealized self-image for the same reason, to unify the personality, but the attempt is doomed because it rests on illusion, an unattainable ideal of absolute perfection rather than a realistic look at strengths and weaknesses.

Tyranny of the shoulds. Trying to reach this impossible ideal, neurotics fall into the tyranny of the shoulds. They tell themselves they should be the best student, spouse, parent, lover, employee, friend or child. Finding their real self so undesirable, they feel they must live up to the idealized image in which they are virtuous, honest, generous, considerate and courageous. In doing so they deny their real selves and try to become what they think they ought to be. They inevitably fail, and end in self-hatred, unable to forgive themselves or others (Kerr).

The neurotic's self-image. Though it does not match reality, the idealized image feels real and accurate to the person who made it. Others easily see through it; the neurotic cannot. It is a model of what the neurotic thinks he or she is, can be or should be. A realistic self-image is flexible and dynamic, changing as the person develops; it reflects strengths, growth and self-awareness, and acts as a goal that both reflects and leads the person. The neurotic self-image is static, inflexible and unyielding: a fixed idea rather than a goal, a hindrance to growth that demands rigid obedience. It is a poor substitute for real self-worth. The neurotic lacks self-confidence because of insecurity and anxiety, and the idealized image blocks correction of these deficits, offering only illusory worth and alienating the person from the true self. Built to reconcile incompatible behaviours, it becomes one more element in the conflict and adds to a sense of futility. The smallest crack threatens the false superiority and security it was meant to provide; Horney likened it to a house full of dynamite, always ready to destroy itself.

Externalization. One defence against the inner conflict caused by the gap between idealized and real self is externalization: projecting the conflicts onto the outside world. The person experiences the conflicts as if they were happening outside and sees external forces as their source. For example, someone who hates himself because of the gap between real and ideal selves may project that hatred onto other people or institutions and believe the hatred comes from them. This may ease anxiety for a while but does nothing to close the gap between the idealized image and reality.

Contrasting the two (a review question). The tyranny of the shoulds turns the conflict inward: the person drives himself to match the ideal and ends in self-hatred. Externalization pushes the conflict outward: the person blames others or outside forces. Both arise from the same gap between the real and idealized self, and neither resolves it.
sections.simple: Everyone forms a picture of themselves. A normal person's picture is realistic and helps them grow; a neurotic's is a fantasy of perfection. Trying to live up to it creates a 'tyranny of shoulds' that ends in self-hatred, and blaming the world for the inner clash is called externalization.
keyPoints: Normal self-image: realistic, flexible, dynamic; a goal that supports self-realization.
Neurotic idealized self-image: based on illusion of perfection; static, rigid; feels real only to the neurotic.
Tyranny of the shoulds: denying the real self to meet the ideal; ends in self-hatred (Kerr).
The idealized image adds to conflict and is fragile, like a house filled with dynamite.
Externalization: projecting inner conflict onto the outside world; relieves anxiety briefly, closes no gap.

sections.heading: Feminine Psychology: Womb Envy, Flight from Womanhood and the Oedipus Complex
sections.detailed:
Horney disagreed with Freud's view of women early in her career. In 1922 she began her own feminine psychology, becoming the first woman to present a paper on the subject at an international psychoanalytic congress, held in Berlin and chaired by Freud himself. Feminine psychology, for Horney, is a revision of psychoanalysis to take in the psychological conflicts built into the traditional ideal of womanhood and women's roles.

Critique of penis envy. She attacked penis envy as based on inadequate evidence, namely Freud's interviews with neurotic women, and interpreted from a purely male viewpoint at a time when women were second-class citizens. Freud had portrayed women as victims of their anatomy, forever envious and resentful of men; he also claimed that women have poorly developed superegos (from inadequately resolved Oedipal conflicts) and inferior body images because they see themselves as castrated men.

Womb envy. Horney turned the argument around: men envy women's capacity for motherhood. She based this partly on the pleasure she said she experienced in childbirth, and she found in her male patients what she called womb envy, describing how surprisingly intense men's envy of pregnancy, childbirth and motherhood appeared once one analysed men after long experience with women. Because men play such a small part in creating new life, they sublimate womb envy and overcompensate by seeking achievement in work (Gilman). Womb envy and its resentment show unconsciously in behaviour that belittles women and keeps them inferior: denying them equal rights, limiting their chances to contribute and downgrading their achievements. Beneath this typical male behaviour lies a sense of inferiority rooted in womb envy.

Why some women feel inferior. Horney did not deny that many women believed themselves inferior. She rejected Freud's claim that this has a biological basis. Women feel unworthy because they have been treated as unworthy in male-dominated cultures; after generations of social, economic and cultural discrimination this self-view is understandable.

The flight from womanhood. Because of these inferiority feelings, women may deny their femininity and unconsciously wish to be men, which Horney called the flight from womanhood (1926). It can lead to sexual inhibitions. Part of the fear comes from childhood fantasies about the size difference between the adult penis and a girl's vagina, centred on injury and painful forced penetration. This produces a conflict between the unconscious wish for a child and fear of intercourse. If strong enough, it causes emotional disturbance in relations with men: such women distrust and resent men and reject their sexual advances.

The Oedipus complex reinterpreted. Horney accepted that children and parents have conflicts but denied they are sexual. Removing sex from the Oedipus complex, she recast it as a conflict between dependence on parents and hostility toward them. Parental behaviour that undermines security breeds hostility, but because the child depends on the parents it cannot express it ("I have to repress my hostility because I need you"). The hostility remains and creates basic anxiety. The result can look just like Freud's Oedipus complex, passionate clinging to one parent and jealousy of the other, but it springs from neurotic conflicts in parent-child interaction. Such feelings are neither sexual, biological nor universal; they arise only when parents undermine the child's security.

What did Freud say about Horney? Freud did not answer her directly or change his Oedipus theory. In a thinly veiled reference, he wrote that it would not be surprising if a woman analyst not convinced of her own wish for a penis failed to weigh that factor in her patients. Of Horney he said she was "able but malicious." Horney was bitter that Freud never accepted her views as legitimate.
sections.simple: Horney rejected Freud's penis envy: she said men envy women's ability to bear children (womb envy) and make up for it by achieving at work and keeping women down. Women who feel inferior do so because of how male-dominated cultures treat them, not anatomy, and some flee from femininity. She also stripped sex out of the Oedipus complex, recasting it as a clash between needing parents and resenting them.
keyPoints: 1922: first woman to present on feminine psychology at an international psychoanalytic congress (Berlin, chaired by Freud).
Penis envy rejected: based on neurotic women and a male viewpoint.
Womb envy: men envy motherhood, sublimate it through work achievement, and belittle women.
Women's inferiority feelings come from cultural discrimination, not biology; can lead to flight from womanhood.
Oedipus complex = conflict between dependence on and hostility toward parents; not sexual or universal.
Freud's response: veiled dismissal; called her 'able but malicious'.

sections.heading: Motherhood or Career? and Cultural Influences on Feminine Psychology
sections.detailed:
Motherhood or career? As an early feminist, Horney (1967) was concerned with the psychological conflicts involved in defining women's roles, contrasting the traditional ideal of womanhood with a more modern one. In the traditional scheme, promoted and endorsed mostly by men, a woman's role was to love, admire and serve her man, and her identity was only a reflection of her husband's. Horney argued that women must find their own identity, as she did, by developing their abilities and pursuing careers. The clash between the traditional and modern roles creates conflicts that some women still struggle to resolve. Writing in the 1980s, the feminist Westkott, drawing on Horney, described modern women as caught between making themselves desirable to men and pursuing their own goals, producing conflicting behaviour (seductive versus aggressive, deferential versus ambitious) and leaving them torn between love and work and dissatisfied with both. Combining marriage, motherhood and career is still hard for some women in the 21st century, as it was for Horney in the 1930s. Her own choice to focus on her abilities and work gave her great satisfaction, yet she kept searching for love and security all her life.

Cultural influences on feminine psychology. Horney recognised that social and cultural forces shape personality and that cultures and social groups view women's roles differently, so there can be many feminine psychologies. She wrote that the American woman differs from the German woman, both differ from certain Pueblo Indian women, and a New York society woman differs from a farmer's wife in Idaho; specific cultural conditions create specific qualities in women as in men.

Example: traditional Chinese society. From as early as the first millennium B.C., women were subordinate to men. Society rested on the belief in two contrasting yet interacting elements, yin and yang. Yang, the male element, stood for everything vital, positive, strong and active; yin, the female element, for what is dark, weak and passive. Over time these formed a hierarchy with men superior. The idea entered the teaching of Confucius (551-479 B.C.), whose thought ruled China for centuries. Women were bound by strict rules to be submissive, obedient, respectful, chaste and unselfish. The Chinese word for woman literally meant "inside person," confining her to the home. According to Loo, a respectable woman was not to be seen or heard; she obeyed her father, then her husband, then her eldest son if widowed. Men were warned not to listen to women, and ambition admired in a man was considered wicked in a woman.

Contrasting this with views of women in contemporary American society, and in a rapidly changing China, supports Horney's position that the feminine psyche is influenced, even determined, by cultural forces.
sections.simple: Horney saw women caught between the traditional role of serving a husband and the modern push for their own identity and career, a conflict Westkott later described as being torn between love and work. She also argued there is no single feminine psychology: each culture shapes women differently. Traditional Chinese society, built on yin-yang and Confucian rules that made women 'inside persons', shows how strongly culture can shape women's lives.
keyPoints: Traditional role: love, admire and serve the man; identity reflects the husband's.
Horney: women should build their own identity through abilities and careers.
Westkott (1986): modern women torn between love and work, dissatisfied with both.
Many feminine psychologies exist because cultures differ (American, German, Pueblo, New York vs Idaho).
Traditional China: yin (female, weak, passive) vs yang (male, strong, active); Confucian rules; woman as 'inside person'.

sections.heading: Questions about Human Nature
sections.detailed:
Horney's image of human nature is considerably more optimistic than Freud's. One reason is her belief that biology does not condemn us to conflict, anxiety, neurosis or universality in personality.

Uniqueness. Each person is unique; there are no universal biological patterns forcing everyone into the same mould.

Nature versus nurture. Neurotic behaviour, when it occurs, comes from social forces in childhood. Parent-child relationships either satisfy or frustrate the child's safety need; if it is frustrated, neurotic behaviour follows. Neuroses and conflicts can therefore be avoided if children are raised with love, acceptance and trust. Social environment, not biology, is decisive.

Ultimate goal: self-realization. Everyone has an innate potential for self-realization, which is the ultimate and necessary goal of life. Our abilities will unfold as naturally and inevitably as an acorn becomes an oak. The only thing that can block this is the thwarting of the childhood need for safety and security.

Role of childhood versus adulthood. Human nature is flexible and not set into fixed shapes in childhood. We can consciously shape and change our personality, and everyone has the capacity to grow, so adult experiences may be as important as childhood ones.

Free will versus determinism. Horney was so confident of our capacity for self-growth that she stressed self-analysis in therapy and in her own life; her book Self-Analysis (1942) argued that we can help resolve our own problems. On this issue she sided with free will: we can shape our lives and achieve self-realization.

Comparison with Freud (a review question). Freud saw personality as driven by biological instincts, fixed by about age 5 and largely determined, with conflict inevitable and universal. Horney saw it as socially shaped, unique, changeable throughout life, guided by an innate urge toward self-realization, and open to conscious change.
sections.simple: Horney was much more hopeful than Freud. She thought each person is unique, neurosis comes from poor parenting rather than biology, and kids raised with love and trust can avoid it. Everyone has a built-in drive toward self-realization, like an acorn becoming an oak, and we can consciously change ourselves throughout life.
keyPoints: More optimistic than Freud: biology does not doom us to conflict or neurosis.
Each person is unique; neurosis results from childhood social forces, avoidable with love, acceptance and trust.
Innate potential for self-realization is life's ultimate goal (acorn-to-oak analogy).
Personality is flexible; adult experiences may matter as much as childhood ones.
Favoured free will; stressed self-analysis (Self-Analysis, 1942).

sections.heading: Assessment in Horney's Theory
sections.detailed:
Horney mainly used Freud's techniques, free association and dream analysis, but modified them. The biggest difference was the analyst-patient relationship. She felt Freud was too passive, distant and intellectual, and saw analysis as an "exquisitely cooperative enterprise" between patient and therapist. She kept a couch but did not use it with every patient. She adopted what she called constructive friendliness, finding by trial and error whether a patient worked better lying down or sitting up and encouraging patients to sit, lie, walk around or do whatever they wished.

Free association. Unlike Freud, she did not use free association to probe the unconscious, because she believed patients could easily distort or hide parts of their inner lives or falsify feelings about remembered events. Instead she focused on patients' visible emotional reactions toward her, which she thought revealed their attitudes toward other people. She did not dig for supposed infantile sexual fantasies; she asked about early life only after assessing present attitudes, defences and conflicts. She believed each attitude or feeling came from a deeper, earlier attitude, which came from a still deeper one, so free association gradually uncovered early experiences and emotions, like peeling the layers of an onion.

Dream analysis. Horney thought dreams could reveal the true self and that they are attempts to solve problems, either constructively or neurotically. Dreams can show attitudes different from those of the self-image. She offered no list of universal dream symbols, insisting that each dream be interpreted in the context of the patient's conflict. She focused on emotional content, holding that the safest clue to a dream lies in the feelings the patient has in the dream.

Self-report inventories. Horney did not use psychological tests, but later researchers built several from her theory:
- The CAD (Cohen, 1967), a 35-item self-report inventory measuring the Compliant, Aggressive and Detached types.
- The Horney-Coolidge Type Indicator (HCTI), a 57-item inventory of the three trends. Research with children and college students confirmed it as a valid measure (Coolidge and colleagues, 2001, 2010). With college students, men scored higher on aggressive and detached scales and women higher on compliance. The trends also related to personality disorders: aggression and detachment correlated highly with psychoticism, and compliance with neuroticism (Coolidge et al.; Shatz).
- The Horney-Coolidge Tridimensional Inventory, a newer version for children and adolescents aged 5 to 17 (Coolidge, Segal, Estey, & Neuzil, 2011).

How her free association differed from Freud's (a review question): no probing of the unconscious, focus on present emotional reactions toward the analyst, present attitudes before childhood, no search for infantile sexual fantasies, and a warm, cooperative rather than distant relationship.
sections.simple: Horney used free association and dream analysis like Freud, but in a warmer, more cooperative way she called constructive friendliness. She watched patients' emotional reactions to her and worked from present attitudes back to childhood, layer by layer like an onion. Later researchers built tests of her three trends, the CAD and the HCTI.
keyPoints: Analysis as a cooperative enterprise; 'constructive friendliness'; flexible use of the couch.
Free association: focus on emotional reactions to the analyst and present conflicts; layers of an onion.
Dream analysis: dreams reveal the true self and attempt to solve problems; no universal symbols; focus on feelings.
CAD (Cohen, 1967): 35 items measuring compliant, aggressive, detached.
HCTI: 57 items; valid; gender differences; links to psychoticism and neuroticism; Tridimensional Inventory for ages 5-17.

sections.heading: Research on Horney's Theory
sections.detailed:
Method. Horney used the case study method, so her work carries the same weaknesses already noted for Freud, Jung and Adler. She refused to take verbatim notes, arguing that one cannot attend wholeheartedly while scribbling, so complete records of her sessions do not exist. Still, she tried to be rigorous: she formed hypotheses, tested them in therapy and held that her data were tested as scientists in other fields test theirs.

Neurotic trends. Caspi, Elder and Bem redefined the trends as moving against people (ill-tempered), moving away (shy) and moving toward (dependent), and compared late-childhood behaviour with behaviour 30 years later. Ill-tempered boys and girls became ill-tempered adults, prone to divorce and downward occupational mobility. Shy boys became aloof adults with marital and job instability, but shy girls showed no such problems. Dependent boys became agreeable, socially poised, warm, giving adults with stable marriages and careers; the opposite held for dependent girls (Caspi, Bem, & Elder, 1989).

Moskowitz and Schwartzman (1989) compared aggressive and detached children aged 7 to 13 with their behaviour 5 to 7 years later. Highly aggressive children had low school achievement and psychiatric problems; detached or withdrawn children had inaccurate, negative self-images. The researchers concluded Horney's types predict later behaviour.

Using the CAD, students heading for helping professions such as nursing and social work scored higher on compliance than those heading for business or science; business students scored higher on aggression; science students scored highest on detachment, consistent with Horney's descriptions (Cohen; Rendon).

In Iran, people high in aggression had significantly more car accidents than those low in aggression (Haghayegh & Oreyzia, 2009).

Feminine psychology. Research bears only indirectly. The classic dream study supporting penis envy (Hall & Van de Castle, 1965) fails to support Horney's challenge to that concept. However, research refuting Freud's claim that women have weak superegos and inferior body images can be taken as support for Horney.

The tyranny of the shoulds. College students recalled three things they had done in the previous week and said whether they did them because they should or because they wanted to. Those who acted more from genuine wanting had significantly higher general life satisfaction than those driven mainly by shoulds (Berg, Janoff-Bulman, & Cotter, 2001).

Neurotic competitiveness. Horney saw neurotic competitiveness, an indiscriminate need to win at all costs, as a major feature of modern culture, comparing such a person to a jockey who cares only about being ahead. Researchers built the Hyper-competitive Attitude Scale (HCA) and the Neurotic Competitiveness Inventory (NCI), rated on a five-point scale from "never true of me" to "always true of me" (Deneui; Ryckman, Thornton, & Butler). High scorers were also high in narcissism, neuroticism, authoritarianism, dogmatism and mistrust, and low in self-esteem and psychological health. People who deliberately avoided competition showed higher neuroticism and less drive to prove themselves (Ryckman, Thornton, & Gold, 2009). Hyper-competitive men were also hypermasculine or macho, seeing women as sex objects deserving neither respect nor consideration. American college students scored higher in hyper-competitiveness than students in the Netherlands, suggesting cultural differences (Dru; Ryckman and colleagues). These findings support Horney's description.

Two types of competitiveness. Researchers distinguished competing to win (CW), aimed at dominating others, from competing to excel (CE), aimed at surpassing one's own goals. Among high school students CE was linked to high self-esteem and low depression. Teen boys scored higher on CW than girls, but girls who scored high on CW showed more depression and loneliness and had fewer close friends (Hibbard & Buhrmester, 2010).

Chapter highlights: high scorers on the aggressive trend may do poorly in school, may have mental health issues, and are likelier to major in business than helping professions; high scorers on neurotic competitiveness tend to be neurotic, narcissistic, authoritarian and low in self-esteem.
sections.simple: Horney's own evidence came from case studies without verbatim notes, so it shares Freud's weaknesses. Later studies support her three trends (they predict adult outcomes and career choices), her idea of the tyranny of the shoulds (doing things because you 'should' lowers life satisfaction) and neurotic competitiveness (linked to narcissism and low self-esteem). Support for her feminine psychology is only indirect.
keyPoints: Case study method, no verbatim notes; same weaknesses as Freud, Jung and Adler.
Caspi, Elder & Bem: ill-tempered, shy and dependent children followed 30 years; gender differences for shy and dependent.
Moskowitz & Schwartzman: aggressive kids had poor school achievement and psychiatric problems; detached had negative self-images.
CAD: helping professions more compliant, business more aggressive, science most detached; Iran: aggression linked to car accidents.
Berg et al.: acting from 'shoulds' lowers life satisfaction.
Neurotic competitiveness (HCA, NCI) linked to narcissism, neuroticism, low self-esteem; CW vs CE (Hibbard & Buhrmester).

sections.heading: Reflections on Horney's Theory
sections.detailed:
Contributions. Horney's contributions are impressive but less recognised in psychology than those of Freud, Jung and Adler. Yet she drew a large public following, partly because of her personal qualities; a student (Clemmens) remembered her wholeness, certainty, dedication and conviction that her ideas could help people in need. Her books are written in a style non-specialists can follow, and her theory has commonsense appeal; many readers find it fits themselves, relatives or friends.

Her ideas may be more relevant to problems of present-day American culture than those of Freud, Jung or Adler. Many personality researchers see the neurotic trends as a valuable way to categorise deviant behaviour, and others accept her emphasis on self-esteem, the need for safety and security, basic anxiety and the idealized self-image.

She significantly influenced Erik Erikson and Abraham Maslow. Maslow adopted her concepts of the real self and self-realization, and her basic anxiety resembles Erikson's basic mistrust.

Criticisms. Although trained in orthodox Freudian theory and grateful to Freud for her foundations, she deviated from psychoanalysis and was heavily criticised by loyal Freudians, who saw her denial of biological instincts and reduced emphasis on sexuality and the unconscious as obvious weaknesses. Her theory is also criticised as less completely and consistently developed than Freud's; some suggest that since Freud's model was so elegant and precise she should have rejected it and started fresh rather than reshaping it. Another criticism is that her observations were too heavily shaped by the middle-class American culture in which she developed much of her theory, though the authors note that all theorists are affected by their class, culture and time.

Renewed interest. Mainly because of the women's movement beginning in the 1960s, her books regained attention. Her writings on feminine psychology and sexuality may be her most influential contribution, still valued by scholars of women's roles more than 50 years after her death (Gilman; Miletic). A biographer (Quinn) said these papers alone would have earned her a place of importance in the history of psychoanalysis. The Karen Horney Clinic (established 1945), which still treats mild to moderate neurotic problems at moderate cost, and the Karen Horney Psychoanalytic Institute, a training centre for analysts, both in New York City, show her lasting impact. A small but loyal group of followers carries on her work, much of it published in the American Journal of Psychoanalysis.
sections.simple: Horney is less famous than Freud, Jung or Adler, but her readable books and commonsense ideas won a big public following, and she shaped Maslow and Erikson. Freudians attacked her for dropping instincts, sex and the unconscious, and others say her theory is less complete and too tied to middle-class America. The women's movement revived interest in her feminine psychology.
keyPoints: Popular, readable, commonsense theory; neurotic trends useful for categorising deviant behaviour.
Influenced Maslow (real self, self-realization) and Erikson (basic anxiety ~ basic mistrust).
Criticised by Freudians for neglecting instincts, sexuality and the unconscious.
Less complete and consistent than Freud's theory; too shaped by middle-class American culture.
Revived by the women's movement from the 1960s; Karen Horney Clinic (1945) and Institute continue her work.

terms.definition: A higher-level need for security and freedom from fear; in Horney's view it dominates childhood and its satisfaction depends entirely on how parents treat the child.
A pervasive, gradually growing feeling of loneliness and helplessness in a hostile world, arising from repressed hostility toward parents; the foundation of neurosis.

The resentment a child feels when parents undermine its security (favouritism, unfair punishment, broken promises, ridicule, etc.); usually repressed out of helplessness, fear, love or guilt, producing basic anxiety.
The four childhood ways of defending against basic anxiety: securing affection, being submissive, attaining power and withdrawing; they seek security rather than happiness.
Self-protective mechanism based on the idea 'if you love me, you will not hurt me'; affection may be sought by pleasing, bribing or threatening others.
Self-protective mechanism of complying with the wishes of one person or everyone, never criticising or offending: 'if I give in, I will not be hurt'.
Self-protective mechanism of compensating for helplessness by gaining success or superiority over others, on the belief that the powerful cannot be harmed.
Self-protective mechanism of becoming psychologically (not physically) independent of others by blunting emotional needs so others cannot hurt you.
Ten irrational defences against anxiety that become a permanent part of personality and drive behaviour; neurotic when pursued compulsively as the only way to resolve basic anxiety.
Three categories of behaviours and attitudes toward oneself and others (toward, against, away from people) that express a person's needs; Horney's 1945 revision of the neurotic needs.
Behaviours and attitudes of the neurotic trend of moving toward people, such as an intense need for affection, approval and a dominant partner.
Behaviours and attitudes of the neurotic trend of moving against people, such as a domineering, controlling manner and a drive for superiority.
Behaviours and attitudes of the neurotic trend of moving away from people, such as an intense need for privacy and self-sufficiency.
In the neurotic, the one neurotic trend that governs behaviour and attitudes toward others because it best controls basic anxiety; the other two are repressed.
To Horney, the basic incompatibility of the three neurotic trends; present in everyone but far more intense in neurotics, and the core of neurosis.
For normal people, a picture of oneself built on a flexible, realistic assessment of one's abilities; for neurotics, one based on an inflexible, unrealistic self-appraisal of absolute perfection.
The full development and use of one's potential; an innate urge and the ultimate goal of life, requiring a self-image that reflects the true self.
An attempt to realize an unattainable idealized self-image by denying the true self and behaving in terms of what we think we should be doing; ends in self-hatred.
A way of defending against the conflict caused by the gap between the idealized and real self-image by projecting the conflict onto the outside world.
Horney's revision of psychoanalysis to cover the psychological conflicts inherent in the traditional ideal of womanhood and women's roles.
Freud's claim that women envy men for possessing a penis; Horney rejected it as based on neurotic women and a male point of view.
The envy a male feels toward a female because she can bear children and he cannot; Horney's answer to Freud's penis envy; men sublimate it through work achievement.
A condition in which women, because of inferiority feelings, deny their femininity and unconsciously wish to be men; can lead to sexual inhibitions.
Analysing one's own problems without a therapist; Horney practised it for life after her failed Freudian analysis and stressed it in her book Self-Analysis (1942).
Adler's notion Horney applied to herself: feeling inferior as a woman and unattractive, she sought superiority by excelling in male-dominated medicine.
Horney's therapeutic attitude of warm cooperation with the patient, including flexibility about using the couch.
A 35-item self-report inventory (Cohen, 1967) measuring Horney's Compliant, Aggressive and Detached types.
A 57-item self-report inventory of Horney's three neurotic trends, validated with children and college students.
Newer version of the HCTI for children and adolescents aged 5 to 17.
An indiscriminate need to win at all costs; Horney saw it as a major feature of contemporary culture.

Horney's research method; shares the weaknesses noted for Freud, Jung and Adler, and she kept no verbatim notes.

examples.title: Compliant trend: the 'yes' friend
examples.text: A student who agrees to every plan, takes the blame for group-project delays and panics if a friend replies late to a message fits Horney's compliant type: security depends on approval, so any hint of rejection feels terrifying.

examples.title: Aggressive trend: the topper who must win
examples.text: A classmate who treats every test as a battle, mocks others' marks and studies only to rank first, not because the subject interests him, shows the aggressive trend: work is a means to superiority, not an end in itself.

examples.title: Detached trend: the hostel loner
examples.text: A student who avoids group outings, refuses to commit to a project team, and insists on logic over feelings in every discussion illustrates movement away from people and the need for privacy and self-sufficiency.

examples.title: Tyranny of the shoulds
examples.text: Someone who believes they should top every exam, be the perfect child and never say no to anyone keeps falling short, and ends up hating themselves. Horney would say they are chasing an idealized self instead of accepting the real one.

examples.title: Externalization
examples.text: A person who cannot accept their own failure to meet impossible standards starts saying 'the professors hate me' and 'the system is against me', placing the conflict outside themselves.

examples.title: Securing affection in childhood
examples.text: A child who keeps giving away toys and sweets to classmates so they will like him is, in Horney's terms, trying to guard against basic anxiety by buying affection.
